name: acyclic-visitor
intent: Decouple a volatile element hierarchy from independently shipped operations by giving each concrete element its own tiny visitor-capability interface and making accept probe for that capability; unlike GoF Visitor, adding an element does not edit or recompile existing visitors, at the cost of runtime misses for unsupported pairs.
problem: The classical Visitor makes the element base depend on a visitor base whose overload set names every concrete element, while every concrete element depends on that visitor base, creating a source-dependency cycle and forcing a sparse operation/type matrix to be maintained as if it were dense. When elements are added by another team, plugin or release, existing visitors should keep compiling and running; when operations are added in separate modules or against a frozen hierarchy, the elements should not be edited. Acyclic Visitor trades compile-time coverage for one capability interface per element and a runtime test in accept.
context: Statically typed object-oriented code with an open or frequently extended element hierarchy, separately deployed operations, and a sparse matrix in which each operation legitimately handles only some elements. It fits when the hierarchy is a frozen API or plugin boundary and incremental compilation, relinking, retesting or redeployment of existing element modules is expensive. The pattern is a source-dependency technique, not a general replacement for tagged-union matching: its payoff tracks the cost of coupling and its risk is the runtime no-op for an unsupported pair.
benefits: Dependencies stay acyclic: the element base depends only on a degenerate visitor base, and each element depends only on its own visitor interface, so a new element never forces existing visitors to be edited or recompiled.

Partial visitation is natural - a visitor implements only the element interfaces it cares about (the sparse-matrix form of the visitor matrix), with no no-op stub methods for elements it does not handle.
Elements and visitors can be compiled, versioned and released independently: visitors ship in their own modules, plugins or third-party packages while the element hierarchy stays untouched.

Both axes stay open at the module level: new elements do not break existing visitors, and new operations do not require editing the elements - the classic Visitor offers only one of the two directions.

Existing callers keep working across element additions: code holding a base-class reference compiles and runs unchanged, and visitors written before the new element remain valid because they simply do not handle it.
Recompilation is minimised in build systems where a header or interface change otherwise cascades through every element derivative and every user of those derivatives.
tradeoffs: The failed type test is silent by default: an element added later is skipped by existing visitors, so what the classic Visitor reports as a compile error becomes a runtime no-op that tests and review must catch.

The dispatch cost is not constant: the time of the cross cast depends on the width and depth of the hierarchy and on the runtime's implementation of it, which Martin calls out as a problem for hard real-time code with predictable latency budgets.

It needs runtime type information and multiple inheritance (or multiple interface implementation) - two features that are controversial, absent in some languages, and awkward to emulate where they are missing.

More types than the classic form: a degenerate base, one interface per element, and a concrete visitor that must declare every element interface it implements; each element also carries a hand-written accept that repeats the same test-and-forward lines.
Static coverage disappears with partial visitation: nothing proves that a visitor which should handle an element does handle it, so correctness migrates from the compiler to tests and review.

The degenerate base must be polymorphic on purpose - in C++ typically a pure virtual destructor - and getting that wrong turns the cross cast into undefined behaviour, so the pattern has a subtle precondition.

Complexity is the price of the acyclic property; Martin's own guidance is that the visitor family is seductive and that something simpler often solves the same problem, so the pattern must earn its keep against a plain method or a closed-set match.

participants.responsibility: Base type of the visited hierarchy; declares accept(Visitor) and otherwise knows nothing about visitors, so it never depends on a concrete visitor or on any operation.

Implements accept by testing the incoming visitor against its own element-visitor interface and forwarding to that interface's visit operation if the visitor supports it; a visitor that fails the test is treated as unable to visit this element.

Degenerate base - an empty marker interface, or an otherwise empty polymorphic base - that exists only as the type accept receives; in languages with runtime type information it must be polymorphic, which is why C++ gives it a virtual (usually pure virtual) destructor.

One abstract visitor per concrete element (E1Visitor, E2Visitor, ...), each declaring exactly one visit operation that takes that element type; the one-to-one mapping between element and interface is what lets a concrete visitor declare support for a subset.

Implements one or more element-visitor interfaces and their visit operations while also deriving from the degenerate base; the set of interfaces it implements is its capability matrix, so a visitor that handles three of ten elements implements exactly three visitor interfaces.

use_cases: Compiler, analyser and code-generation tooling where AST node types are added over several releases while passes, printers and checks ship as separate modules or plugins.
Plugin architectures where third-party visitors must keep working when the host adds a node type, and must not be recompiled, re-signed or redeployed for the addition.
Large C++ code bases with expensive incremental builds, where a change to the visitor base hierarchy would otherwise trigger a rebuild of every element derivative and its users.

Sparse operation/type matrices in which each visitor legitimately applies to a handful of element types (configure for DOS, configure for Unix, configure for X) and stub methods for the rest are pure noise.
Frozen or third-party element hierarchies that may not be edited but still need new operations added from the outside - the operations live entirely in the new module.
Long-lived products in which elements and operations are versioned and released independently and the binary or source compatibility of the element hierarchy matters.
Document object model (DOM) processing where new node types are added by a standards body but existing serializers, validators and analytics must not be recompiled or re-deployed.
Static analysis and linting frameworks where new check visitors are shipped independently from the core engine and the rule repository, while the abstract syntax tree schema is versioned separately.

Serialization frameworks where schema evolution adds new record types while existing serializers and deserializers (as visitors) continue to function for types they know, with a graceful no-op for unknown types rather than a runtime crash.
UI event-routing systems where new widget types are introduced but existing event handlers (as visitors) handle only the widgets they understand, and the routing layer is never recompiled.

LLVM/Clang tooling: clang::RecursiveASTVisitor gives independently written analyses Visit* hooks over a framework-owned AST; use this mature CRTP visitor when the framework's traversal contract is enough, rather than claiming it is Martin's cross-cast form.

Roslyn analyzers: Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharpSyntaxWalker/CSharpSyntaxVisitor lets analyzer packages override only relevant syntax-node visits while the framework owns the immutable syntax-tree classes.

Rust enum matches, Kotlin sealed hierarchies and TypeScript discriminated unions are the modern replacement when the variant set is intentionally closed and exhaustive operation coverage is more valuable than independent element releases.
avoid_when: The element set is closed and small - use sealed-hierarchy-exhaustive-match, a Rust enum match, a Kotlin sealed-class when or a TypeScript discriminated union so the compiler can reject a missing case instead of turning it into a runtime no-op.

One operation family runs over a stable hierarchy - classic Visitor keeps one complete visit interface and lets the compiler force every visitor to acknowledge each element, whereas acyclic Visitor pays for sparse runtime capability tests.

Both the element and operation axes must remain open with static type safety - prefer extensible-visitor or object-algebra encodings when their generic machinery fits, instead of accepting acyclic Visitor's silent-miss risk.
Dispatch must be predictable in time or extremely cheap - a type tag or dispatch table keyed by the element kind avoids hierarchy-size-dependent RTTI cross-casts.

The language already provides multiple dispatch or generic functions (Clojure-style multimethods, Python functools.singledispatch) - use the language feature instead of hand-built interfaces and casts.
The operations are really transformations over data you own - model the data as a closed union and write plain functions over it, which the host language can check exhaustively.
The real problem is that one class grew too many methods - split the class or extract a smaller collaborator instead of externalising behaviour behind a visitor.
The element set is closed and small - a sealed hierarchy with exhaustive matching, a union type, or a language enum gives compile-time coverage with far less machinery.
One operation family over a stable hierarchy - the classic Visitor keeps the compiler forcing every visit method to exist and costs less indirection.
Dispatch must be predictable in time or extremely cheap - a type tag or a dispatch table keyed by the element kind avoids the hierarchy-size-dependent cast cost.
anti_patterns: Choosing acyclic Visitor when the element set is stable: unlike classic Visitor, it pays for a degenerate base, per-element interfaces and runtime misses for a problem that does not exist.
Ignoring the failed capability test, with no log, assertion, status or error hook, so an unhandled element/visitor pair disappears and the visitor quietly does half its job.
Making the degenerate base non-degenerate: adding a visit method or catch-all default recreates the classic Visitor coupling and hides which elements a visitor really supports.
Implementing every per-element visitor interface for completeness, which restores visitor-to-element coupling and throws away the sparse partial-visitation benefit.
Using acyclic Visitor to justify cast-based control flow elsewhere: its capability test is a boundary contract for one operation, not a general branching tool.
Using the pattern in a shallow hierarchy where recompilation is negligible: the degenerate base, per-element interfaces and cross-casts cost more than simply rebuilding.
design_principles: Open/closed principle: both the element hierarchy and the set of operations are open for extension without modifying existing code.

Acyclic dependencies principle: the point of the pattern is that the source-dependency graph between modules has no cycles, so elements and visitors can be compiled, tested and released independently.
Interface segregation: one minimal visitor interface per element instead of a single fat visitor interface that every visitor must implement in full.
Dependency inversion: elements depend on their own abstract visitor interface rather than on concrete operations, and operations depend on the abstract element type.
Single responsibility: each visitor carries exactly one operation, and each element only knows how to hand itself over to a capable visitor.
best_practices: Keep the visitor base empty and polymorphic on purpose; in C++ give it a pure virtual destructor and document the reason in a code comment — it is the load-bearing RTTI enabler, not a cosmetic choice.
Treat the failed test as a first-class event: log, increment a counter, or assert so that missing coverage surfaces in tests, telemetry and production dashboards rather than vanishing silently.
Give every element exactly one visitor interface and keep accept as the three-line test-and-forward pattern so that adding a new element stays mechanical and local.

Decide by which axis varies: use acyclic visitor when elements vary over time; use classic Visitor when operations vary over a fixed, stable element set and compile-time exhaustiveness checking is worth the coupling cost.

Benchmark the dynamic_cast before committing it to a hot path: its cost grows with hierarchy width and depth, and a kind-tag dispatch table is often 10-100x faster for large hierarchies (benchmarks show dynamic_cast can be 25-77x slower than a type-index dictionary, and a well-designed template visitor_cast can be within 2-4x of the classic form).

Prefer pointer-based cross-casts (dynamic_cast<X*>(&v)) over reference-based (dynamic_cast<X&>(v)) to get a null pointer on failure rather than std::bad_cast, which would require exception handling on every accept path.

Cover both handled and unhandled cases in tests for each element's accept: call accept with a visitor that implements the element's interface and assert the operation runs; call with a visitor that does not and assert the no-op is observable (logged, counted or returned).
When element counts are large, generate the per-element visitor interfaces and accept methods with a source generator, macro or code-generation build step rather than maintaining them by hand.

For plugin architectures, version the degenerate visitor base and each element-visitor interface independently; a version mismatch on the visitor base should produce a clear runtime error rather than a silent null from a failed cross-cast.

Consider the const variant of each accept overload (accept const Visitor&) alongside the mutable form; in C++ a separate Visitor<const T> interface hierarchy that derives from the non-const form keeps const-correctness without duplicating the visitor implementations.

If RTTI is disabled or unavailable, replace dynamic_cast with a std::unordered_map<std::type_index, void*> registry keyed by the concrete visitor type; the lookup is slower than dynamic_cast but the pattern remains implementable in RTTI-free environments.
pitfalls: Silent unhandled element: When a new element type is added to the hierarchy, existing visitors that were written before the element was conceived simply skip it at runtime. The classic Visitor would report this as a compile error; acyclic visitor turns it into a runtime no-op. Without deliberate test coverage for the new element, this can ship to production as a latent bug. Mitigation: Maintain an integration test suite that traverses representative object graphs containing all known element types and asserts that every visitor produces observable output (a log entry, a counter increment, or a return value) for each element it claims to handle. Add new test cases at the same time as new element types.

dynamic_cast cost on hot paths: The cross-cast is not a constant-time operation in most implementations. Its cost grows with the width and depth of the inheritance hierarchy, and it is significantly slower than a simple virtual call or a dispatch-table lookup by a kind tag. In latency-sensitive or tight-loop code this overhead is measurable and often prohibitive. Mitigation: Profile before adopting the pattern in any path that will be called millions of times per second. For hot paths, use a hand-written kind tag or a std::unordered_map<std::type_index, void*> registry as a faster alternative to dynamic_cast. Templated visitor_cast implementations (as in Alexandrescu's Modern C++ Design) can reduce the overhead to within 2-4x of classic virtual dispatch.

Reference-based cross-cast throwing std::bad_cast: Using dynamic_cast<X&>(v) instead of dynamic_cast<X*>(&v) throws std::bad_cast when the cast fails. This pollutes every accept path with exception-handling overhead and couples the element code to the exception type, defeating the purpose of the clean null-check pattern. Mitigation: Always use the pointer form: auto* av = dynamic_cast<VisitorFor<Circle>*>(&v); if (av) av->visit(*this);. Reserve reference-based casts only for contexts where failure is truly exceptional and should propagate upward.

Non-polymorphic degenerate base: In C++, dynamic_cast requires its operand to be a polymorphic type (at least one virtual function). If the degenerate visitor base is made non-polymorphic to keep it 'pure', the cross-cast in every accept method becomes undefined behaviour, not a failed cast. Mitigation: Give the degenerate base exactly one pure virtual destructor: virtual ~VisitorBase() = 0;. This is the canonical RTTI enabler and costs nothing at runtime (the destructor call is trivial). Document the purpose in a comment so future maintainers do not remove it.

Restoring coupling through the element-visitor interface: Each element-visitor interface (e.g. CircleVisitor) declares a visit(Circle) method that takes the concrete element type by reference or pointer. This creates a coupling from the visitor side to the concrete element — but the element side now also depends on its own visitor interface name. If the visitor interface is placed in the same header as the concrete element, the element has a compile-time dependency on the visitor interface, though not on any concrete visitor implementation. Mitigation: Place each element-visitor interface in its own header, included only by the elements that need it and by the concrete visitors that implement it. This preserves the acyclic property at the module level even though the element must name its visitor interface.

Non-obvious branch ordering with inheritance: When concrete elements inherit from other concrete elements (e.g. Square inherits from Rectangle), a visitor that handles Rectangle will also succeed for Square unless the Square-specific branch is tested first. This ordering dependency is invisible to the compiler and easy to get wrong, especially when the hierarchy is deep. Mitigation: Write accept tests from most-derived to least-derived, or use a dynamic_cast to the narrowest type first. Add unit tests that verify the correct branch fires for each concrete type, including subtypes, to catch ordering mistakes before they ship.

Code bloat from per-element boilerplate: Every element needs its own visitor interface and its own accept method. In a hierarchy of 50 element types, this means 50 small visitor interfaces and 50 three-line accept methods. Hand-written, this is a copy-paste maintenance hazard; even with a code generator, the generated code can obscure the intent of the pattern. Mitigation: Generate the per-element interfaces and accept methods programmatically using a build-time code generator, a macro system, or a template mixin. In C++, CRTP-based mixins can reduce the boilerplate to a single inheritance declaration per element. Review the generated code in code review to ensure it is auditable.

Choosing runtime misses for a closed hierarchy: Wrong move: use acyclic Visitor for a small, owned set of variants. How it fails: adding a variant leaves old visitors compiling and silently skipping it, so a missing operation is discovered only by tests or production behavior. Instead: use a sealed hierarchy, enum/union and exhaustive match when the set is intentionally closed. Mitigation: Make the openness decision explicit in the design review: retain acyclic Visitor only when independently released elements are a real requirement; otherwise let the compiler enforce coverage.

Treating an unsupported pair as success: Wrong move: leave the failed per-element capability test as an unobservable no-op. How it fails: a visitor that was supposed to process a new element returns normally after doing nothing, and callers cannot distinguish success from omission. Instead: make the miss observable with a returned status, counted/logged event or deliberate assertion at the boundary. Mitigation: Define the unsupported-pair policy for each operation: reject it, record it, or explicitly allow it as a best-effort no-op; never let the default branch make that decision accidentally.

Confusing a framework visitor with the acyclic form: Wrong move: assume that an API called RecursiveASTVisitor or SyntaxVisitor inherits acyclic Visitor's independent-element guarantee. How it fails: a framework may use a classic overload set, CRTP or generated dispatch and still require visitor updates when its node model changes. Instead: inspect the framework's actual extension and versioning contract before promising plugin compatibility. Mitigation: Use LLVM/Clang and Roslyn as proven visitor implementations and alternatives, not as evidence that every visitor API has acyclic dependency behavior; document whether node additions are source- or binary-compatible.

related_patterns_notes.visitor: classic double-dispatch with one visitor interface method per element; choose it when the element set is stable and compile-time coverage matters.
related_patterns_notes.extensible-visitor: a type-safe extensible visitor/algebra encoding intended to keep both axes open; prefer it when runtime capability misses are unacceptable.
related_patterns_notes.double-dispatch: dispatches on receiver and visitor types but does not by itself remove the classic Visitor dependency cycle.
related_patterns_notes.capability-query: asks an object whether it supports an operation; acyclic Visitor narrows that idea to per-element visitor interfaces and accept dispatch.
related_patterns_notes.sealed-hierarchy-exhaustive-match: closes the variant set so the compiler can enforce coverage, the opposite openness trade-off from acyclic Visitor.
related_patterns_notes.dispatch-table: maps a tag or type key to handlers with explicit lookup costs; it can replace RTTI cross-casts on hot paths.
related_patterns_notes.extension-object: keeps optional operations in separate extension objects; unlike acyclic Visitor, it need not route through every element's accept method.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: wraps one object to add behavior along its call path; it does not select an operation by the visited element's concrete type.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: encapsulates one interchangeable algorithm behind a stable interface; it is not a sparse element/operation matrix.
related_patterns_notes.object-algebras: encode constructors and operations with generic algebras and avoid accept methods, addressing the expression problem with stronger static extensibility.
related_patterns_notes.std-variant-std-visit: C++ closed tagged-union visitation with compile-time alternatives; use it instead when variants are owned and intentionally closed.
